summary: NASA plans its Moon Base near the lunar south pole, where the Sun never rises above about 7° and kilometre-long shadows decide where to land, drive and work. Earth analog sites are usually chosen for geology and looks; whether the light matches is rarely checked. P.E.N. (Planetary Environmental Navigator) is an open web app that compares every 6 km window of 14 Earth regions with 6 Moon Base sites and 3 Mars sites, by terrain and by low-Sun light, using NASA LRO and MRO and ESA Copernicus elevation data and an exact cast-shadow model. Tested blind, it ranks Pu’u Hiwahine on Mauna Kea, where NASA, CSA and DLR rehearsed a lunar-polar mission in 2012, #1 of 10,424 Earth windows for Malapert Massif (p = 0.004). Its light model matches NASA’s LOLA illumination map (ρ = 0.92–0.99). Every match comes with a dossier of what Earth cannot reproduce, a live hazard check from NASA EONET, and a Mission view that gives field teams the exact date and hour to rehearse, as a calendar file. It runs in any browser and scales to all of Earth’s land.
details:
What it does. P.E.N. (Planetary Environmental Navigator) finds the exact places on Earth where a team can rehearse the Moon Base, and when. At the lunar south pole the Sun never rises above about 7°, so kilometre-long shadows decide where to land, drive, place solar panels and walk. Earth test sites are usually chosen for geology and looks; whether the light matches is rarely checked. P.E.N. checks both.

How it works. We put NASA elevation models (LRO LOLA for 6 Moon Base sites, MRO CTX for 3 Mars sites) and ESA Copernicus DEM for 14 Earth regions on one 30 m grid, and cut Earth into 10,424 windows of 6 km. For each window we measure 5 terrain features and exact cast shadows with the Sun at 2° and 5° (a running-maximum algorithm, exact and one pass per row). Each feature difference is scaled by its spread across Earth, and the result is a 0–100 score per dimension that says what matches and what does not.

Evidence. Tested blind, P.E.N. ranks Pu’u Hiwahine on Mauna Kea, where NASA, CSA and DLR rehearsed a lunar-polar mission in 2012, #1 of 10,424 windows for Malapert Massif. A null test against random windows gives p = 0.004 (0.025 corrected for 6 lunar targets). Its light model matches NASA’s LOLA illumination map (Spearman ρ = 0.92–0.99 at all six sites). We also report where it is weak: for Mars the score does not separate the known sites (AUC 0.33–0.50).

Benefits and impact. Field-test planners get the exact 6 km site, the week and the hour for rover-vision, EVA-lighting and landing-hazard tests. Mission plans a rover route on both terrains and exports the matching date as a calendar file (.ics). Every match has a dossier of what Earth cannot reproduce (LRO Diviner shows the Moon Base is 95–132 K colder than our coldest Earth region) and a live hazard check from NASA EONET. In Mexico, El Pinacate ranks in the top 3 % for 4 Moon Base sites. The method scales to all of Earth’s land in under 4 hours on 64 cores.

Creativity. P.E.N. adds light to the analog question, validates it against NASA’s own maps, and turns a match into a date. The web app runs the shadow algorithm live in the browser on the real terrain.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, pandas, Matplotlib) for the pipeline; TypeScript with Vite, MapLibre GL, Three.js, ECharts and KaTeX for the web app on GitHub Pages; pytest, Node tests and Playwright in GitHub Actions. No special hardware.

What we considered. Same resolution for every body, no labels in scoring (known sites only test the result), every number traced to data and checked automatically, honest limits, and an app that works on a phone with no install.
